verdict_reasoning: The proposal fails at level 1b on already-exists-1 and demand-1. Message #1 does not say what a three-column, SQL-only view gives over a user-written UNION ALL or a documentation example, and it shows no demand beyond the author, who himself asks whether the view is useful. Neither objection is fatal and the cost is small, so this is "not now, justify and show demand", not a rejection. Confidence is low because the thread is one message with no replies and the verdict rests on absence of evidence.

brief.title: Add a pg_stat_progress overview view listing all backends currently reporting command progress
brief.problem: Today, to find which operations are reporting progress, a user has to query each pg_stat_progress_* view one by one. The author wants a single place to discover active progress-reporting operations across the cluster. The audience is implied rather than stated: DBAs and monitoring tools. The longer-term aim is to make cluster operations easier to discover and monitor.
brief.proposed_design: Add a new system view, pg_stat_progress, defined in system_views.sql. It has one row per backend that is reporting command progress, across all databases. It has three columns: pid, command (the command family), and progress_view (a regclass naming the detailed progress view to consult). The view reuses pg_stat_get_progress_info() and the existing progress reporting permissions, with no backend C changes. datid/datname were considered and left out because some tracked operations (for example base backups) cover the whole cluster. The pg_stat_progress_cluster compatibility view does not add extra rows. Commands that do not support progress reporting do not appear. Catversion is bumped, regression output in rules.out is updated, and a new TAP test is added in test_misc.
user_visible_surface: Column pg_stat_progress.command (text), with values ANALYZE, VACUUM, CREATE INDEX (includes REINDEX), BASEBACKUP, COPY, REPACK (includes CLUSTER and VACUUM FULL), DATACHECKSUMS
Column pg_stat_progress.progress_view (regclass) naming the detailed per-command progress view
Overview columns visible to all users; detail access follows the existing per-view permission rules
New documentation section 'Active Command Progress' in monitoring.sgml
author_claims: Finding active progress reports currently requires querying each pg_stat_progress_* view separately
pid, command and progress_view are the minimal common fields
Implementation reuses existing infrastructure with no backend changes
datid/datname are omitted because some operations, such as base backups, cover the whole cluster
Documentation and tests are included; build, regression, isolation and new TAP tests passed locally
Longer-term aim: easier discovery and monitoring of cluster operations, and extending progress reporting to more commands
brief.thread_state: Only the first message is visible; no one has replied yet. The author asks for feedback on usefulness and on the column choice. CFbot reports that the patch needs a rebase.
unclear: Whether the view could include more common fields (e.g. datid, relid, phase, query start time) or why they are excluded beyond the datid/datname reasoning
How the view handles possible future progress command types (whether the command-to-view mapping must be manually maintained)

Whether the overview row is shown even when the user lacks permission to see details, and whether showing pid/command to all users is a desired disclosure (the docs say the columns are visible to all users)
Whether the value of a three-column overview beyond a UNION query a user could write themselves has been weighed
Why the DATACHECKSUMS and REPACK command families are present, and which other patches or base version this depends on
Performance or cost of the view when there are many backends
What the rebase conflict reported by CFbot is

objections.title: A three-column view that any user can already write as a UNION over the existing pg_stat_progress_* views
objections.failure_scenario: A DBA or monitoring tool queries pg_stat_progress, sees pid 12345 with command COPY, and still has to query pg_stat_progress_copy to learn anything useful: which relation, which phase, how far along. The tool therefore keeps its existing per-view queries, and the new view saves it nothing. The project meanwhile carries a permanent catalog view and a frozen three-column API. When a later release wants the overview to carry phase or relid, it has to change a published view shape instead of having designed it once. The same three columns are already one query away today: SELECT pid, 'VACUUM', 'pg_stat_progress_vacuum'::regclass FROM pg_stat_progress_vacuum UNION ALL ... over the seven existing views, or one call to pg_stat_get_progress_info() per command type.
objections.argument: The patch adds no backend changes, and the commit message says so: it only reuses pg_stat_get_progress_info() and the existing views. So the whole feature is a SQL definition in system_views.sql that a user, a monitoring tool or a documented example query could hold just as well. The existing progress views already expose pid. The tool that wants the detail must already know every progress view, so knowing the list of views is no extra burden. Message #1 justifies the view only by "finding active progress reports currently requires querying each pg_stat_progress_* view separately". It does not weigh this against the UNION a user can write, and it does not say what a consumer does with pid/command/progress_view alone that it could not do before. A committer would likely ask: what does core placement give here that a documentation example or a monitoring tool's query lacks? The only candidate visible in the material is that core updates the list automatically when new progress commands appear. But that list is kept by hand in system_views.sql, much as a user would keep it. The narrowest columns were chosen on purpose, which is exactly what makes the view a near-duplicate of the existing UNION idiom rather than an extension of it.
objections.author_must_show: Show what the overview gives that a UNION ALL over the existing progress views (or a documented example query) cannot. This could be common fields that are awkward to assemble today, such as phase, relid/datid where they apply, or a normalized fraction-complete. It could also be a concrete monitoring workflow, or field reports of users or tools that need command discovery without detail. Alternatively, reduce the patch to a documentation example of the UNION query.

critic.reasoning: The patch is SQL only and the author does not weigh it against a user-written UNION ALL or a documentation example, so the question of what core placement adds is unanswered in the material. Two parts should be softened. A core view does give something a user's UNION lacks: it tracks the set of progress views per major version, whereas a hand-written UNION breaks when a view such as the REPACK or DATACHECKSUMS one is absent or added. And the 'frozen three-column API' is overstated, because columns can be added later. The core ask remains valid: show a workflow, or richer common columns. This is a 'not now / justify' objection, not a rejection.

objections.title: No evidence that anyone besides the author wants this; the only stated need is the author's own
objections.failure_scenario: The view is committed for v20 with no user asking for it. Monitoring tools such as dashboards and exporters already query each pg_stat_progress_* view, because they need the counters and not only the existence of an operation. They keep doing so. The view then sits in system_views.sql and rules.out, and its command list has to be updated by whoever adds progress reporting for the next command. Years later a committer finds no user of it and still has to defend it, while no one can remove it without breaking whoever did start using it.
objections.argument: The material contains no field report, no -general or -bugs thread, no second person asking for it, and no comparison with another system. Message #1 gives the whole motivation in one line: 'finding active progress reports currently requires querying each pg_stat_progress_* view separately'. It then asks the list for 'feedback on the usefulness', so the author has not established usefulness either. No one has replied yet. The audience (DBAs, monitoring tools) is implied, not stated, and the stated longer-term aim of extending progress reporting to more commands is a separate proposal that this view does not deliver. Under rubric item 3 this is 'it would be nice' plus 'I needed it', not demand. The honest result is 'not now, show demand', not a rejection.
objections.author_must_show: Concrete demand from people other than the author. Examples: a monitoring tool such as an exporter, pgwatch-style collector or cloud console that would replace its per-view queries with this view; -general or -bugs threads where users could not find a running operation; or a reviewer or committer in the thread saying they would use it. A stated user workflow in which the overview alone, without the follow-up query, answers the user's question would also help.

critic.reasoning: The material shows no demand beyond the author's one-line motivation, and the author himself asks whether the view is useful. The thread is four days old with no replies, so nothing in it lowers this concern. The objection frames the outcome correctly as 'not now / show demand' rather than rejection, and it must not by itself raise the verdict.

other_surviving.title: The column name 'command' already means something else in every pg_stat_progress_* view that has it
other_surviving.failure_scenario: A monitoring tool joins pg_stat_progress to pg_stat_progress_create_index USING (pid, command), or filters WHERE command = 'REINDEX'. The join drops every row whose detail command is 'REINDEX', 'REINDEX CONCURRENTLY' or 'CREATE INDEX CONCURRENTLY', because the overview only ever says 'CREATE INDEX'. The filter returns nothing. The same mismatch hits COPY (detail 'COPY FROM'/'COPY TO' against overview 'COPY') and CLUSTER/VACUUM FULL (detail command against overview 'REPACK'). A DBA on call sees CREATE INDEX in the overview and goes looking for a CREATE INDEX statement, when the session is actually running REINDEX CONCURRENTLY. Nobody notices until a dashboard silently undercounts. Once the view ships, the vocabulary cannot be fixed without breaking whatever has been built on it.
other_surviving.argument: The documentation hunk defines pg_stat_progress.command as a 'command family' with values ANALYZE, VACUUM, CREATE INDEX, BASEBACKUP, COPY, REPACK, DATACHECKSUMS. It notes that 'CREATE INDEX' includes REINDEX and that 'REPACK' includes CLUSTER and VACUUM FULL. The existing detailed progress views that have a column named command use it for the actual command being run, at a finer grain. So the same column name, within the same view family, means two different things, and the values look similar but do not match. Some values (BASEBACKUP, DATACHECKSUMS) are not SQL command spellings; they read like internal progress-type names exposed as a user-facing contract. Message #1 asks specifically for feedback on the column choice, and nothing explains why this departure from the existing views' naming is justified. A committer would likely ask for a distinct name (for example command_type or progress_type), or for values that match what the detailed views report.
other_surviving.author_must_show: Rename the column, for example to progress_type or command_type, so it does not collide with the existing 'command' columns. Alternatively, report the same fine-grained values the detailed views report. State whether the family strings are a stable contract, and how they map to the detailed views' command values.

critic.reasoning: The facts hold. pg_stat_progress_create_index, pg_stat_progress_copy and pg_stat_progress_cluster already have a command column that carries the finer-grained actual command, so the overview reuses the name with a coarser meaning, and the author gives no justification while asking for feedback on the columns. One sub-point must be dropped: BASEBACKUP, CREATE INDEX and the like are the existing cmdtype argument strings of pg_stat_get_progress_info(), so those spellings copy existing practice and are not the patch's fault. The JOIN USING (pid, command) scenario is contrived, but the WHERE command = 'REINDEX' confusion is plausible. A rename solves it.

other_surviving.not_ranked_reason: level 2 is above the failing level 1b: not evaluated (base-up stop rule)

other_surviving.title: Hand-maintained command-to-view mapping in system_views.sql will silently go stale when new progress commands are added
other_surviving.failure_scenario: Release N+1 adds progress reporting for a new command, for example a new ProgressCommandType and its own pg_stat_progress_foo view. That is exactly the extension the author says is the longer-term aim in message #1. The committer updates the C enum, pg_stat_get_progress_info's name lookup, the new detailed view and its docs. Nobody remembers to also add a branch to pg_stat_progress's definition. Regression and TAP tests still pass, because the overview test only covers the commands it already knows. After release, a DBA or a monitoring tool that relies on pg_stat_progress as the single place to discover active operations (the stated purpose) never sees the new command. A long-running operation goes unnoticed, and the bug is reported months later as 'pg_stat_progress misses X'.
other_surviving.argument: The patch touches only SQL (system_views.sql), docs, rules.out and a TAP test. There are 'no backend changes' (message #1, commit message). So the list of command families (ANALYZE, VACUUM, CREATE INDEX, BASEBACKUP, COPY, REPACK, DATACHECKSUMS), their text labels and the regclass of each detailed view must be enumerated by hand in the view definition. The docs hunk also lists the families by hand and special-cases the pg_stat_progress_cluster compatibility view. That makes a second, parallel registry of progress command types that lives far from the C enum, with nothing tying the two together. This is the item 9 pattern: an update that future patches must make, that a reviewer is likely to miss, and nothing fails loudly if someone forgets. The value of an 'overview' view lies entirely in being complete, so silent incompleteness defeats the feature.
other_surviving.author_must_show: Show a mechanism that makes omission fail loudly. One option: derive the command name and view from the backend (for example, have the progress infrastructure expose the command type name for every slot, so the view needs no per-command branch). Another: add a regression or TAP check that compares the set of ProgressCommandType values or pg_stat_progress_* views against what pg_stat_progress can return, and that fails when a new type is added without updating the overview.

critic.reasoning: I tried 'copies existing practice': every new progress command already needs a hand-written view in system_views.sql and a string branch in pg_stat_get_progress_info(). That does not rescue it, because forgetting those makes the new feature visibly absent, while forgetting the overview branch is silent and nothing in the described tests would catch it. Since the view's stated purpose is complete discovery and the author plans to add more commands, the item 9 concern is specific and real. A cross-check test or a backend-derived mapping fixes it.

other_surviving.not_ranked_reason: level 2 is above the failing level 1b: not evaluated (base-up stop rule)

refuted.title: A permanent system view for a three-column UNION, with no demand shown
refuted.failure_scenario: The project ships pg_stat_progress, and from then on carries it in rules.out, monitoring.sgml, and every future progress-reporting patch (see the first objection). Monitoring tools that already query the individual pg_stat_progress_* views keep doing so, because they need phase and counters anyway, and those are absent from the overview. The view ends up used mainly by people who could have written the UNION over pg_stat_progress_* views themselves. Meanwhile, the first request for datid, relid or phase reopens the column-set debate on a view that can no longer drop or rename columns.
refuted.argument: Message #1 states the problem as 'finding active progress reports currently requires querying each pg_stat_progress_* view separately'. It offers no field report, no -general thread and no monitoring-tool request, and it asks the list whether the view is useful at all. The three columns (pid, command, progress_view) carry no counters, so every real consumer still has to go to the detailed view. Everything the view returns can already be obtained from the existing views or pg_stat_get_progress_info() by a user-written query. This is a candidate for 'not now / show demand' rather than a rejection: the cost is small but permanent, and the benefit is unproven.
refuted.author_must_show: Evidence that monitoring tools or DBAs want this overview: tool maintainers asking for it, -general or -bugs reports, or comparable features elsewhere. Also a column set justified by actual consumers, for example why phase or relid are not common enough to include, so that the view shape is not revisited right after release.

critic.reasoning: Duplicate of demand-1 for the item 3 no-demand point, and of already-exists-1 for the UNION and column-set point. Its claim that the view 'can no longer drop or rename columns' is also overstated for the stated worry, since adding datid, relid or phase to a system view in a later major release is routine.

refuted.title: Three columns that any DBA can already get with a short UNION ALL, and the user still has to run a second query
refuted.failure_scenario: A DBA sees a long-running maintenance operation and queries pg_stat_progress. They get pid=12345, command='COPY', progress_view='pg_stat_progress_copy'. That tells them nothing about phase, relation, database or how far it has got. They now have to run the second query the docs show, which is the same query they would have run without the new view. Users who wanted a single glance at what is running and how far along it is get no closer to that. Users who only want a list of operations can already write a UNION ALL over the seven pid columns, or check pg_stat_activity.query.
refuted.argument: The documentation hunk shows the intended workflow as two steps: 'SELECT * FROM pg_stat_progress; SELECT * FROM pg_stat_progress_copy WHERE pid = 12345;'. So the view saves only the discovery step, and that step has a trivial user-level workaround. The patch is SQL only: it touches system_views.sql and has 'no backend changes'. Anything it computes is therefore expressible by a user or a tool today. datid/datname were deliberately dropped (message #1), and relid, phase and start time were not offered. That removes the fields that would make the overview worth looking at on its own. A committer would likely ask what problem a three-column list solves that pg_stat_activity plus the existing views do not.
refuted.author_must_show: Either (a) a concrete use case where pid, command and progress_view alone is the answer the user needs, or (b) a version with enough common fields to avoid the second query in the common case, for example datid (nullable for cluster-wide operations), relid, phase and a start or elapsed time. In both cases, a comparison against the UNION ALL query users can write today, showing what the built-in view adds.

critic.reasoning: Duplicate of already-exists-1: the same item 2 argument that the three columns are obtainable by a UNION ALL and a second query is still needed. already-exists-1 states it more completely.

touch_points.label: catalog changes
touch_points.reason: Adds the system view pg_stat_progress in system_views.sql, with a catversion bump and a rules.out change.

touch_points.label: security / privileges
touch_points.reason: The docs say pid and command are visible to all users, across all databases; detail access relies on the existing per-view permission rules.

touch_points.label: maintenance burden ("who maintains this in 10 years")
touch_points.reason: The command-family list and the command-to-view mapping are kept by hand in system_views.sql and monitoring.sgml, and must be updated for each new progress command.

touch_points.label: doesn't fit what Postgres is about (extension / external tool / already solved)
touch_points.reason: The view is SQL only over pg_stat_get_progress_info(), so a user, a monitoring tool or a documentation example can already produce the same three columns with a UNION ALL.

questions: What does a core pg_stat_progress view give that a UNION ALL over the existing pg_stat_progress_* views, or a documented example query, does not? Name a workflow in which pid, command and progress_view alone answer the user's question without the second query.
Who besides you wants this: which monitoring tool, -general or -bugs report, or user would replace per-view queries with this view?
Why does the overview carry no further common fields, for example datid (NULL for cluster-wide operations), relid or phase, so that the common case needs no second query?

When a new progress command type is added, what makes a missing branch in pg_stat_progress fail loudly: a backend-derived mapping, or a test that compares the view against the set of progress command types?

Why is the column named command when the existing command columns in the create_index, copy and cluster progress views carry the finer-grained actual command (REINDEX, COPY FROM, VACUUM FULL)? Would a different name such as progress_type or command_type be acceptable?

committability.owner_note: It needs a committer who knows the command progress reporting infrastructure and the monitoring system views. Nobody has replied in the visible thread.
committability.liability: The owner signs for the view's name, its column set and the command-family strings as a user-facing contract for monitoring tools, for as long as the view exists. The owner also signs for keeping the hand-maintained command-to-view mapping complete every time a progress command is added.
committability.author_follow_up: Weak positive sign: in message #1 the author asks for feedback and states a longer-term aim to extend progress reporting to more commands. There is no later message, and the rebase CFbot requested on 2026-11-10 has not been posted yet.

not_now.evidence_that_would_change_it: Any of the following would change the answer. (1) A monitoring tool maintainer or several independent users stating in the thread that they would use the overview. (2) -general or -bugs reports where users could not find a running operation. (3) A concrete workflow in which the overview alone, without the follow-up query, is the answer. (4) A revised column set, such as nullable datid, relid or phase, that a user-written UNION ALL cannot easily assemble. A stated reason why a core view beats a documentation example would also help, for instance that it tracks the set of progress views per major version.

provisional_note: The level 2 objections that survived (standards-compat-1 on the command column name, maintenance-fit-1 on the hand-maintained mapping) were not evaluated because the proposal stops at level 1b. Without the code it could not be checked that the view definition leaks nothing beyond what the existing progress views show, whether the TAP test covers every progress command type, or what the REPACK/DATACHECKSUMS dependency and the rebase conflict are.
disclosure: Prepared by an AI harness; treat as a devil's advocate, not a verdict.

roaster_notes.note: No precedent found. None of the 15 retrieved rows proposes a unified or overview progress view, and none records a reason that would still apply here. [P5] (VACUUM Progress Checker, Returned with feedback, 2016) is in the same area, but it was an earlier per-command progress mechanism, not an overview over existing ones, and it records no objection or reason. So it cannot carry an objection and is not listed as a related prior attempt. [P11] touches monitoring docs linkends and records no reason. [P2], [P3], [P6] and [P8] concern pg_stat_statements. The rest ([P1], [P4], [P7], [P9], [P10], [P12], [P13], [P14], [P15]) share only keywords such as 'view' or 'stats'. Message #1, the only message, points to no earlier discussion of the same idea, and no replier has spoken yet. From the prior-attempts angle there is nothing to raise. Other angles will cover the open questions: value over a user-written UNION, manual upkeep of the command-to-view mapping as new progress commands are added, disclosure of pid/command to all users, and the dependency on REPACK/DATACHECKSUMS from other patches.

Only one objection from the standards and compatibility angle, and it is fixable.

Checked and found no problem:
- No new SQL syntax, keywords or GUC.
- No change to existing views or behaviour, so existing queries are unaffected.
- pg_dump is not involved, since this is a system view.
- The name pg_stat_progress fits the existing naming scheme. Tools that match names with LIKE 'pg_stat_progress_%' will not pick it up by accident.
- Disclosure of pid and command family seems to match what the existing progress views already expose to unprivileged users, but this cannot be confirmed without the code.

Left to other angles:
- Desirability against a user-written UNION.
- Manual upkeep of the command-to-view mapping when progress types are added.
- The dependency on REPACK and DATACHECKSUMS being present in the base version.

From the replication and on-disk angle this proposal has no persistent or cross-node state to object to. It adds one SQL view in system_views.sql over the existing in-memory pg_stat_get_progress_info() shared-memory data, with a catversion bump.

- **On-disk format / pg_upgrade:** no heap, index, SLRU, control-file or relation-file change. The view lives in the system catalogs that initdb creates, so pg_upgrade does nothing special and old data is unaffected.
- **WAL / replication:** no WAL record, no change to replay, and nothing a standby or subscriber has to agree on. Progress views are per-node, in-memory and not replicated, so a mixed-version rolling upgrade is not affected.
- **Wire protocol:** unchanged.
- **ABI / extension API:** the brief says there are no backend C changes, so no struct, hook or signature changes. The catversion bump only rules out back-patching, which is normal for a new system view.
- **Pairings (item 14):** no state is created that would need cleanup on error, DROP, crash or promotion. Rows disappear when the backend stops reporting progress.
- **Not checked without the code:**
  - whether the hard-coded command-to-view mapping fails loudly when a new progress command type is added. This is a maintenance concern for another angle.
  - whether the view behaves sensibly on a hot standby, for example for a base backup taken from a standby.
  - the cause of the CFbot rebase failure.

From the security and privileges angle I found nothing that justifies an objection.

1. The view discloses nothing new. According to the patch prose, it is built only on pg_stat_get_progress_info() and the existing progress-reporting permissions, with no backend C changes. As I understand current behaviour, each pg_stat_progress_* view already shows a row per reporting backend to every user. The pid and database stay visible, and relid and the counters are nulled when the caller lacks pg_read_all_stats or the same role. So any user can already learn "backend X is running a VACUUM/COPY/CREATE INDEX" by querying the individual views or by running the UNION themselves. The new view puts in one place what is already readable; it adds no new class of information. pg_stat_activity also already exposes pid and backend_type to all users. The documented choice "These columns are visible to all users" copies existing practice. By the rubric's own lowering signal, it is not this patch's fault.

2. The patch drops fields rather than adding them. It omits datid/datname, relid and phase, so it exposes less than the detailed views do. Detail access stays governed by those views.

3. No escalation path. It is a plain system view with no SECURITY DEFINER, no user-supplied code, no search_path exposure, and no involvement in maintenance commands, pg_dump or replication apply. RLS, column privileges and leakproofness do not apply.

4. No unprivileged DoS. It is a bounded scan over the backend status array, the same cost as the existing views.

Limits of this check, without the code:
- I could not confirm that the view's definition does not call the progress function in a way that exposes relid or params unfiltered, for example by deriving progress_view from a privileged column. The commit message says it reuses the existing permissions, so I take that at face value.
- I could not check how the DATACHECKSUMS and BASEBACKUP rows are filtered, since they depend on patches not shown.

Those are code-level questions, not design objections. Desirability concerns, such as value beyond a user-written UNION and the mapping that must be maintained by hand, belong to other angles.

No hot-path concern: the view is pure SQL over pg_stat_get_progress_info() and adds no per-backend or per-tuple cost for non-users. Its cost scales with the number of command families times backend slots, and only when it is queried. Exposing pid and command to all users mirrors what the existing per-command progress views already expose, so I raise no security-fit objection. No new external dependency is involved. The precedents retrieved (pg_stat_statements, the VACUUM progress checker, the pg_hba view and others) have no recorded reasons that apply, so none are cited. Could not check without the code: whether the TAP test already enumerates all ProgressCommandType values, and what the CFbot rebase conflict is (likely its dependency on the REPACK and DATACHECKSUMS work).

Only one objection from this angle. I know of no extension or external tool that provides exactly this view, so I name none. The existing alternative is the plain SQL UNION over the pg_stat_progress_* views, or pg_stat_get_progress_info() called per command type. Whether the hand-kept command-to-view mapping drifts as new progress commands are added is a maintenance question for another angle. So is whether showing pid/command to all users is an acceptable disclosure.

The cost side looks small: SQL only, no backend C changes, existing permissions reused, so the costs fall almost entirely on maintainers and not on non-users' hot paths. The objections are therefore 'not now, show demand', not 'reject'. Out of scope for this angle and left to others: whether the command-to-view mapping is something future progress patches will forget to update, and whether exposing pid and command to all users is an acceptable disclosure.
